evidence.text: The entry catalogs 行 under oracle-bone script, bronze inscriptions (including inscription 集成06305), Chu manuscripts, small seal script, and Shuowen. It supplies a primary-reference trail for the graphic sequence, though the browser exposed labels rather than the glyph images, so I did not independently inspect those images.
evidence.title: 漢字「行」：字形演變

evidence.source: Fudan University Center for Research on Excavated Texts and Ancient Chinese Characters, Guo Lihua
evidence.field: discussion of oracle-bone 行; cited examples 屯2178 and 合集24391
evidence.text: The author identifies the oracle-bone graph as a crossroads and argues its original graphic sense was ‘road’; she cites oracle-bone contexts meaning ‘meet on the road’ and ‘a rhinoceros is on the road.’ She treats verbal ‘walk/go’ as an extension from ‘road,’ and cites later 詩經 and 呂氏春秋 examples of 行 meaning road. This is a scholarly interpretation, not an uncontested chronology of the spoken senses.
evidence.title: 郭麗華：《甲骨文字典》釋義補正五則

evidence.source: Chi-hsiung Cheng et al., University of Chicago Center for East Asian Studies archive
evidence.field: §2 graphic analysis and usage, PDF pp. 4–5
evidence.text: The paper reports oracle-bone forms as a four-direction crossroads, with Western Zhou bronze forms continuing the shape and Chu/Qin manuscript variants also recorded. It lists oracle-bone verbal examples (including inscriptions 21901, 24445, and 33033), and later bronze examples: movement in mid-/late-Western Zhou inscriptions and 德行 in Warring States inscriptions and Guodian Chu slips. It notes that the concrete road-shaped graph could represent both road and movement; thus the graph’s pictorial shape does not by itself establish which spoken sense came first.
evidence.title: 「行」字意義的變遷

evidence.source: Chi-hsiung Cheng et al., University of Chicago Center for East Asian Studies archive
evidence.field: §3 sound and meaning analysis, PDF pp. 6–8
evidence.text: The authors survey four later rhyme-book sound/meaning groupings: 胡郎切 for rank/row; 戶庚切 for walking/going; 下浪切 for order; 下更切 for conduct/action. They propose semantic and phonological relationships among these readings but explicitly frame parts of the ordering as inference and acknowledge that readings in the Jingdian Shiwen do not conclusively settle the chronology. Their discussion presents possible Sino-Tibetan comparisons involving 行 and 胻 as a debated proposal, not an established derivation.
evidence.title: 「行」字意義的變遷

evidence.field: 行部 entry; Han-dynasty lexical/structural account
evidence.text: The entry says 人之步趨也。从彳从亍 (‘human walking, stepping; from 彳 and 亍’) and assigns 行 as the base for its character family. This is an early Han lexicographic analysis, not independent confirmation that the oracle-bone graph originated as a compound of the two modern-looking parts. Duan Yucai’s later note glosses 彳 as small steps and 亍 as stopping a step, then lists extensions including inspection, rows, affairs, and conduct.
evidence.title: 說文解字「行」

evidence.text: A Unicode proposal reports current readings for 行 as háng, hàng, xìng, xíng and proposes changing xìng to héng in that particular dictionary-derived field. This is evidence of multiple modern/lexicographic readings and field-specific variation; it is not a substitute for the current kMandarin character record or evidence for ancient sound relations.

evidence.source: University of Chicago Center for East Asian Studies archive
evidence.text: The authors report Warring States 德行 examples from the 中山王圓壺 and 中山王鼎 and Guodian Chu slips. They infer a path from road/movement toward action or conduct, but acknowledge that the language history cannot be read mechanically from the graph. Their account cautions against treating a gloss list as a dated semantic sequence.

gaps: The available paleographic database page listed script categories and inscription references, but its glyph images were not actually inspected in this research session; detailed stroke-by-stroke change and any graph corruption remain unverified.

Sources disagree or leave open whether the spoken verb ‘go/walk’ historically preceded the noun ‘road,’ despite the crossroads graph strongly depicting a road. The Fudan author argues road → walk; the Chicago paper discusses both and cautions that graph shape alone cannot order the spoken senses.

The dossier’s specific account that 行 originally represented a word glossed ‘place’ and was later borrowed for ‘go’ is not established by the inspected primary and scholarly sources. The unrelated borrowed-word proposal comparing Khmer/Burmese forms was not independently corroborated; source-word chronology and a secure sound match remain unresolved.

The Shuowen 彳 + 亍 component account is a historical Han interpretation. The early forms are described as a whole crossroads graph; this research does not establish 彳 and 亍 as original semantic subcomponents or as phonetics.

The official Unicode per-character Unihan page for 行 could not be accessed. Local supplied row supports Mandarin xíng, but external character-specific verification remains incomplete. No sound-array component is proposed, and no Baxter–Sagart transcription is used as a new sourced claim.
